body.text: Modern physical infrastructure relies on precision systems such as Environmental technology to deliver scale safely. Here is how engineers balance thermodynamics, material limits, and lifecycle cost.

Environmental technology (or envirotech) is the application of one or more of environmental science, green chemistry, environmental monitoring and electronic devices to monitor, model and conserve the natural environment and resources, and to curb the negative impacts of human involvement.
The term is sometimes also used to describe sustainable energy generation technologies such as photovoltaics, wind turbines, etc.
Purification and waste management
Air purification

Air purification describes the processes used to remove contaminants and airborne pollutants to reduce the potential adverse effects on humans and the environment. The process of air purification may be performed using methods such as mechanical filtration, electrostatic filtration ionization, activated carbon adsorption, photocatalytic oxidation, and ultraviolet light germicidal irradiation.
Environmental remediation

Environmental remediation is the removal of pollutants or contaminants which are harmful to people and the environment. The environment includes groundwater, surface water soil or sediments and is done using various methods including soil excavation, soil stabilization, and groundwater treatment.

Water remediation mainly consists of treating agricultural, human consumption, and industrial water to remove any chemical, biological, or radiological contamination using physical, chemical, electrochemical and biological methods.
Sediment remediation consists of removing contaminated sediments. Is it similar to soil remediation except it is often more sophisticated as it involves additional contaminants.
Solid waste management

Waste-to-energy technologies have shown to be promising in better managing solid waste and being more environmentally conscious. Most waste-to-energy methods fall into the categories of either biochemical or thermochemical processes depending on the composition of the waste.
Thermochemical processes, such as gasification, pyrolysis, and incineration, rely on the decomposition of solid waste to produce heat, oil, or gas.

Advances in waste-to-energy technologies relying on thermochemical processes have led to more efficient means of generating products and reducing emissions, with incineration facilities turning to emissions control technology to lower air pollution, while gasification and pyrolysis facilities have found ways to produce higher quality oil and biogas.

Biochemical methods, including composting, aerobic composting, anaerobic composting, and vermicomposting, degrade organic compounds in solid waste. In aerobic composting, for example, aerobic microbes decompose organic solid waste into primarily carbon dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, and nitrate.
AI and ML

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods have recently shown to be effective in managing solid waste. For example, AI methods in some municipalities are used to collect, sort through, and classify waste as "glass, plastic, and other biodegradable materials," allowing for more efficient and effective management of solid waste.

Hybrid techniques, which are combinations of various individual AI methods, have shown to be more effective than stand-alone methods by addressing their shortcomings. The use of ML in solid waste management can lead to cost savings, particularly for waste management facilities, and more efficient and environmentally friendly waste disposal.
A 2021 study developed an image processing method to detect non-biodegradable waste, in the categories of glass, metal, and plastic, from waste bins so that it can be easily separated.

A ML model was trained on images of all three categories of non-biodegradable waste, and the validity of the model was tested using a raspberry pi camera. The 2021 study found that the ML model accurately identified metal 75% of the time, plastic 65% of the time, and glass 60% of the time.
Drone technology

Drone technologies and unmanned aerial vehicles have also been used at solid waste landfills. They have been used to study "spatial and volumetric characteristics of landfills", record emissions of landfill gas, and monitor compliance with landfill regulations. A 2023 study applied drones to identify and classify waste in garbage bins.
The drone collected image and video that was then used to inspect every part of the city remotely and better manage solid waste.

Some key challenges and unsolved issues in managing solid waste are the lack of sorting systems that can organize waste and enable appropriate disposal and the lack of "predictive maintenance systems for waste collection vehicles and treatment facilities."
E-waste recycling

Electronic waste, also known as E-waste, is one of the fastest growing types of solid waste with an annual growth rate of 3% to 5%. In traditional e-waste recycling, electronic waste is "disassembled, crushed, and sorted in the factory" to separate the different parts and materials found in the waste.
Hazardous components are then "stored and supervised", metals are extracted using advanced techniques, such as pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy, and plastics are recycled into new products.

A 2024 study investigated the application of photochemistry and sonochemistry, among other methods, for e-waste recycling. The researchers found that photocatalysis with the use of solar energy was a "green approach" to managing e-waste, however the method led to limited metal collection.
Sonochemistry allowed for better metal recovery, and the use of ultrasonication coupled with other processes, such as photochemistry, showed potential in effectively managing e-waste.
Bio-metallurgy and supercritical fluid treatment

Techniques such as bio-metallurgy and supercritical fluid treatment, particularly using supercritical carbon dioxide as a solvent, have also been used to treat and extract materials from electronic waste.

Bio-metallurgy, or bioleaching, involves the use of microorganisms, such as fungi, to recover raw materials from e-waste and is a more environmentally conscious and less costly process than other methods of treating e-waste. The microorganisms generate "organic acids and redox-active compounds" that allow for efficient metal recovery without toxic byproducts.

Advancements in biotechnology, such as genetically engineered strains of microorganisms and nanotechnology, have also improved efficiency, quantity of metal recovered, and viability of bio-metallurgy processes. However, the adoption of bio-metallurgy faces issues such as the inherently slow nature of the process and microbial toxicity.

Supercritical fluid treatment is a process based on taking advantage of the properties of materials above their critical point, including their critical temperature and critical pressure, to extract metals or other substances from a starting material. Supercritical carbon dioxide is specifically used in green chemistry because it is non-toxic, non-flammable, and not costly to obtain.
Biodegradable devices

Biodegradable devices, such as mechanical energy harvesters, energy storage, and sensors designed using biodegradable materials, can also help to slow e-waste production. AI can also advance research into biodegradable electronic devices by synthesizing properties of biodegradable materials and how they degrade over time.

Some barriers to developing biodegradable devices exist including the lack of understanding of mechanisms for biodegradation and of synthetic biodegradable polymers, the environmental impact of more toxic elements such as molybdenum (Mo) and tungsten (W), and the high cost and short supply of magnesium (Mg), which is a widely used biodegradable material.

A 2026 study found that restrictive random-access memory (RRAM) devices were successfully created on "eco-friendly, biodegradable, and flexible substrate," a key advancement in the development of biodegradable devices.
The devices are able to retain data well and are operationally stable in addition to being decomposable in water-rich soil, showing the device's ability to reduce long-term environmental impact.
Bioremediation

Bioremediation is a process that uses microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, plant enzymes, and yeast to neutralize hazardous containments that can be in the environment. This could help mitigate a variety of environmental hazards, including oil spills, pesticides, heavy metals, and other pollutants.

Bioremediation can be conducted either on-site ('in situ') or off-site ('ex situ') which is often necessary if the climate is too cold. Factors influencing the duration of bioremediation would include to the extent of the contamination, environmental conditions, and with timelines that can range from months to years.
Sustainable energy

Concerns over pollution and greenhouse gases have spurred the search for sustainable alternatives to fossil fuel use. The global reduction of greenhouse gases requires the adoption of energy conservation as well as sustainable generation.
substantially reducing methane emissions from melting perma-frost, animal husbandry, pipeline and wellhead leakage.

Since fuel used by industry and transportation account for the majority of world demand, by investing in conservation and efficiency (using less fuel), pollution and greenhouse gases from these two sectors can be reduced around the globe.

Advanced energy-efficient electric motor (and electric generator) technology that are cost-effective to encourage their application, such as variable speed generators and efficient energy use, can reduce the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) and sulfur dioxide (SO2) that would otherwise be introduced to the atmosphere, if electricity were generated using fossil fuels.
